title: '<span class="spasticity-module-title">Spasticity</span><span class="spasticity-subsection-title">Clinical Presentation</span>'
---

The severity of symptoms of spasticity ranges from mild stiffness or tightening of the muscles to uncontrollable and painful spasms.

## Evaluation

Evaluation should focus on:

- Symptom onset, with special focus on motor weakness, altered sensation, pain, bowel and bladder dysfunction, and sexual function.
- Potential triggers and the underlying disease. Common triggers include skin disease, ingrown toenails, constipation, withdrawal from or initiation of new drugs, infections, and ill-fitting medical devices.
- Family history.

New-onset spasticity could arise following a stroke or traumatic brain injury. Progressive or worsening symptoms may occur with disorders such as multiple sclerosis, while cerebral palsy results from a non-progressive brain injury, although its clinical manifestations can change over time.

Patients may complain of difficulty sleeping due to muscle tightness or pain. They may also have trouble completing activities of daily living.

## Physical Examination

A complete neurological examination is indicated for a patient presenting with spasticity.

It is very important to distinguish between spasticity and rigidity. With rigidity, resistance to movement is constant throughout passive motion. Spasticity produces velocity-dependent resistance to passive movement, often with a characteristic catch and release.

### Observation

- **Thumb-in-palm posture:** Characteristic of spasticity. It is due to excessive thumb adduction and finger flexion, producing a fist with the four fingers wrapped tightly around the thumb.
- Abnormal posturing due to muscle stiffness, particularly involving the shoulder adductors, elbow flexors, wrist and finger flexors, and forearm pronators.

### Reflexes

Hyperreflexia is an expected finding in the affected limb. The muscle contracts much more briskly than normal. A positive Babinski sign may also be present.

### Strength and Tone

The clasp-knife phenomenon is a characteristic finding. The limb has a sudden decrease in resistance as passive movement continues. It feels like opening and closing a pocket knife, hence the name.

Clonus is also a common finding on examination. This presents as alternating contractions and relaxations of agonist and antagonist muscle pairs due to exaggerated stretch reflexes.

Spastic co-contractions occur as abnormal antagonist contractions during voluntary agonist effort.

Spastic dystonia is persistent muscle contraction at rest, resulting in a fixed posture that is relieved by passive stretching.

## Modified Ashworth Scale

The Modified Ashworth Scale is commonly used to grade the severity of spasticity.

::: {.mas-table}

| Grade | Description |
|-|---------|
| 0 | No increase in muscle tone |
| 1 | Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch and release or minimal resistance at the end of the range of motion when the affected part is moved in flexion or extension |
| 1+ | Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch, followed by minimal resistance throughout the remainder of the range of motion, but the affected part is easily moved |
| 2 | More marked increase in muscle tone through most of the range of motion, but the affected parts are easily moved |
| 3 | Considerable increase in muscle tone; passive movement is difficult |
| 4 | Affected part is rigid in flexion or extension |

:::
